c.tagline: Sun-soaked university city near the Med, built around a grand medieval square.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are metered; fixed tariffs apply for airport runs.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number; 15 reaches the SAMU ambulance service, 17 the police, and 18 the fire brigade.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing in the centre and around the station

hood_desc: Montpellier's medieval historic core around the grand Place de la Comédie, a maze of pedestrian lanes lined with cafes, boutiques, and mansions; the best walkable base for first-timers.
Ricardo Bofill's monumental neoclassical quarter of wide boulevards and colonnades running from the old town to the Lez river; central, modern, and well served by tram.
An arty, leafy neighborhood just north of the center full of markets, independent cafes, and artists' studios; a relaxed, bohemian local feel.
A contemporary riverside district along the Lez with bold modern architecture and green spaces, popular with students and young families; lively bars and dining.
Calm residential streets below the Saint-Clément aqueduct and the Peyrou promenade, home to a beloved twice-weekly market; quiet and distinctly local.
lodging: Grand Hôtel du Midi Montpellier - Opéra Comédie
Campanile PRIME - Montpellier Est Le Millénaire

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, as everywhere in France.

transit.hours: TaM trams run roughly 4:30am-1am (later on weekends), with buses on similar hours and a few night services; the four tram lines cover almost everything a visitor needs.
transit.note: TaM runs four colour-coded tram lines plus a dense bus network; the compact Écusson old town is largely pedestrian and best explored on foot.
transit.pay: Buy tickets from tram-stop machines or the TaM app and validate on boarding; a single ride is about €1.60 and a day pass about €4.20. Contactless bank-card tap-on is being rolled out.

bus: Montpellier Sabines coach station (Occitanie liO regional coaches)
FlixBus / BlaBlaCar Bus stops at Sabines
train: Gare Montpellier Sud de France (high-speed, southeast edge)

transit.m: Navette Aéroport shuttle (line 620) to Place de l'Europe, then tram to center (~30-40 min total)
Tram line 1 from Place de l'Europe to the city center (~15 min)

tip.r: Service is included by law (service compris); rounding up or leaving a euro or two for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Tielle setoise
food.desc: Small domed pie from nearby Sete, stuffed with octopus and squid in a spicy tomato sauce under a lattice crust. Eaten warm or cold.

places.name: La Tielle Setoise
places.note: Dedicated tielle maker on avenue du Pont Juvenal, baking the Sete classic daily.

places.name: Halles Castellane
places.note: Covered market where several traiteur stalls sell tielles fresh from the oven.

places.name: Halles Laissac
places.note: Rebuilt market hall with seafood traiteurs stocking tielles and other Sete specialties.

food.name: Brasucade de moules
food.desc: Thau lagoon mussels grilled on a flat plancha over vine cuttings, splashed with garlic, herb and olive oil marinade. A summer beach ritual.

places.name: Marche du Lez
places.note: Open-air food market complex where grill stalls fire brasucade plancha at weekends.

places.name: Palavas-les-Flots seafront
places.note: Line of beach cabanes doing brasucade and grilled fish through the warm months.

places.name: Bouzigues waterfront cabanes
places.note: Shellfish farmers' huts serving their own mussels straight off the plancha.

food.name: Petit pate de Pezenas
food.desc: Cylindrical hot pie with a sweet-savoury filling of minced mutton, lemon zest, brown sugar and spice, said to come from an Indian cook's recipe.

places.name: Halles Castellane
places.note: Charcuterie and traiteur stalls keep the little Pezenas pies alongside regional pates.

places.name: Marche des Arceaux
places.note: Tuesday and Saturday market with producers bringing bakes from the Herault villages.

places.name: Maison Alary
places.note: Long-standing Pezenas bakery treated locally as the reference for the sweet mutton pies.

food.name: Huitres de Bouzigues
food.desc: Plump, briny oysters farmed on ropes in the Etang de Thau, usually served raw by the dozen with lemon and a glass of local white.

places.name: Halles Castellane
places.note: Oyster stalls shuck Thau oysters to eat standing at the counter with wine.

places.name: Halles Laissac
places.note: Fishmongers with a small raw bar; good value dozens at lunchtime.

places.name: Marche du Lez
places.note: Weekend oyster bars pairing Bouzigues shells with Picpoul by the glass.

food.name: Seiche a la rouille setoise
food.desc: Cuttlefish or squid stewed in the saffron-garlic rouille sauce of Sete, thickened with aioli and served with rice or potatoes.

places.name: Setori
places.note: Montpellier address built around Sete cooking, rouille and macaronade included.

places.name: Halles Laissac
places.note: Traiteur counters ladle out rouille setoise by the tub to take away.

places.name: La Calanque
places.note: Sete institution for rouille and other lagoon-and-sea classics.

food.name: Grisettes de Montpellier
food.desc: Tiny dark honey-and-liquorice sweets said to date to medieval pilgrims, sold in little tins as the city's own confection.

places.name: Office de Tourisme boutique
places.note: Reliable stock of authentic Montpellier grisettes in gift tins.

places.name: Halles Castellane
places.note: Confectionery stalls sell grisettes loose alongside regional nougat and candied fruit.

places.name: Old-town confiseries, rue de l'Argenterie
places.note: Cluster of sweet shops in the lanes off Place Jean Jaures carrying the local tins.

food.name: Picpoul de Pinet
food.desc: Crisp, lemony white wine grown on the shores of the Etang de Thau and the standard partner for the region's oysters and mussels.

places.name: Chai Christine Cannac
places.note: Long-running wine bar and cellar strong on Languedoc growers, glasses and bottles.

places.name: Halles Castellane
places.note: Market wine counter pours Picpoul to drink with oysters bought a few metres away.

places.name: Marche du Lez
places.note: Several wine bars in the market complex list local Picpoul by the glass.

food.name: Muscat and cartagene
food.desc: Sweet fortified local wines: Muscat de Frontignan or Lunel as aperitif or dessert, and rustic cartagene made from grape juice and marc.

places.note: Herault vignerons sell muscat and homemade cartagene direct at the market.

places.name: Chai Christine Cannac

places.name: Halles Laissac

landmarks: Place de la Comédie
One of Europe's largest pedestrian squares sweeps from the ornate opera house to the Three Graces fountain, the effervescent stage of Montpellier life.
Promenade du Peyrou
A regal 17th-century esplanade crowned by a Louis XIV equestrian statue and a hexagonal water tower, with views stretching to the Cévennes and the sea.
Saint-Clément Aqueduct (Les Arceaux)
An 18th-century double-tiered aqueduct marches nearly a kilometer through the city on elegant arches, sheltering markets and pétanque games below.
Cathédrale Saint-Pierre
Two colossal rocket-like pillars support the porch of this fortress-cathedral, a brooding 14th-century Gothic giant attached to Europe's oldest medical school.
Musée Fabre
One of France's richest fine-arts museums outside Paris displays Delacroix, Courbet, and a luminous wing devoted to hometown abstract master Pierre Soulages.
L'Écusson (Historic Old Town)
Montpellier's medieval core is a shield-shaped maze of golden-stone lanes, hidden hôtels particuliers, and buzzing café terraces best explored on foot.
Arc de Triomphe (Porte du Peyrou)
This 1693 triumphal gate glorifying Louis XIV marks the grand entrance to the old city; climb it for rooftop panoramas over terracotta tiles.
Jardin des Plantes
Founded in 1593 for medical students, France's oldest botanical garden remains a romantic tangle of ancient trees, greenhouses, and shaded walks.
Antigone District
Architect Ricardo Bofill's monumental neoclassical quarter unfolds in theatrical postmodern symmetry from the old town to the River Lez.
Château de Flaugergues
The finest of Montpellier's 18th-century 'folies', this aristocratic wine estate pairs terraced French gardens with tastings on the city's edge.

train.note: Montpellier has two stations: the central Saint-Roch, in the middle of town at the end of the tram lines, and Montpellier Sud de France, an out-of-town stop about 7 km away on the Nimes-Perpignan bypass line, linked by tram 1. Around four direct trains a day run to Barcelona in under 3 hours - some are Renfe AVE services sold on renfe.com, others SNCF TGVs sold on SNCF Connect, and the fares are not interchangeable. Direct TGVs also run north to Brussels-Midi and Luxembourg from Sud de France. Paris is about 3h15m and Lyon 1h40m. Check which of the two stations your ticket uses, as they are 20 minutes apart.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the Gare Routiere immediately beside Saint-Roch station, so the walk between train and bus is a couple of minutes. Barcelona takes around 5-6 hours by coach against under 3 by train, so the bus is the budget option. Cars liO regional coaches (https://www.lio-occitanie.fr/) cover Sete, Nimes, the Herault villages and the coast at a low flat fare paid on board. International tickets are booked online only; carry ID for Spanish departures.

intl.to: Bejaia & Skikda (Algeria) - sails from Sete, about 25 minutes by train from Montpellier
Bastia & Ajaccio, Corsica (France), Porto Torres, Sardinia (Italy) & the Balearics - sails from Sete

ferry.note: Montpellier itself is about 10 km inland with no port; its ferry terminal is effectively Sete, 25 minutes away by frequent TER train. Corsica Linea runs the Algerian crossings from Sete, taking around 24 hours and sailing once or twice a week, while Corsica Ferries has added seasonal Sete departures for Corsica, Sardinia and the Balearics. Corsican and Sardinian sailings are mostly summer-only, so check dates before planning around them. Vehicles and cabins need booking well ahead in July and August, and the Algerian routes require a visa and a long check-in.

half.name: Sète
half.blurb: A canal-laced fishing port on the Mediterranean known as the Venice of Languedoc, with an active harbor, oyster beds, and a Saturday market.

half.name: Nîmes
half.blurb: A Roman city with the well-preserved Arena of Nîmes amphitheater and the Maison Carrée temple, plus the classical Jardins de la Fontaine gardens.

half.name: Camargue and Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer
half.blurb: A wetland delta of salt flats and marshes where wild white horses and pink flamingos roam near the beach town of Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer.

half.name: Pic Saint-Loup Valley
half.blurb: A limestone-ridge wine valley north of the city, home to vineyards producing some of the Languedoc's most respected reds.

half.name: Béziers
half.blurb: A hilltop town on the Orb River with a fortified cathedral overlooking vineyards and the nine-lock Canal du Midi staircase at Fonséranes.
